Latin.note: The Greek temple-precinct assault is not explicitly expressed in this Latin interval; Hyrcanus’s retreat and detention of the family survive.
Greek §85 additionally describes prisoners taken. This Latin interval explicitly retains the three thousand killed, with no separate capture count here.
The oath and concealed beam survive in this Latin interval; the explicit statement that Eleazar alone knew the secret is not separately expressed here.
The Latin shortens the statement about sacred public money; the eight hundred talents and contextual inference survive.
The Latin compresses the ethnarch’s administrative functions to a short description of the ruler.
The Latin retains the Memphis response and subsequent visit across a paragraph boundary. Greek §132’s separate statement that the preceding group obeyed is not explicitly expressed here.
Greek’s opening description of Hyrcanus’s inattention and the leaders’ fear is compressed out; the explicit charge survives.
The Latin departure and later-summons decision survive. The transmitted oboediret lacks the Greek section’s negation; it is preserved without emendation.
The Latin annual-payment clause names ioppenses as paying Jerusalem; Greek §202 excludes Joppa from the Jerusalem payment. The Latin wording and the sabbatical exception are preserved.
The tithe to Hyrcanus and his sons survives. The Greek Sidon second-year quarter-of-seed provision is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.

The Jewish-association exception survives. The transmitted non prohibuit nec ... parare iussit does not separately reproduce Greek’s full paired exception for contributions and shared meals; no wording is supplied.
Subiugo etiam preserves the introduction of the appended decree. Greek’s explanatory purpose and final as-follows formula are compressed out here.
The Latin collective uel reliquo senatu replaces the continuation of the named-witness list. It supplies collective correspondence; the individual Greek §220 names are not reproduced.

The resolution of Dolabella and Antony survives. Greek §221’s preceding final witness Publius Serrius is not individually expressed in this shortened Latin list; the displayed interval begins with the consuls.
The collective Senate-presence formula replaces the detailed witnesses in Greek §229. Its individual names are not supplied here. Balgus begins the distinct salutation assigned to §230.

Text corresponding to Niese §238 is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The detailed witness list has no identifiable counterpart between the surviving exemption and date in §237 and Lentulus’s decree notice in §240. The cause is unknown.

Text corresponding to Niese §239 is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The detailed witness list has no identifiable counterpart between the surviving exemption and date in §237 and Lentulus’s decree notice in §240. The cause is unknown.
Prytanis’s complaint and the customary harvest reference survive. Greek’s expressly named sabbath and ancestral-rites restrictions are compressed to the Latin’s general inquietudinem.
The hearing and decision survive. The Latin ends with ne prohiberentur, without separately expressing Greek’s final object concerning customary practices.
The request for a decree copy and envoys, and to preserve and increase friendship, survives. Greek’s final become-a-cause-of-good phrase is not separately expressed here.
The Abraham-era friendship recollection survives. Greek’s preceding reciprocity-of-reward phrase is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
The grant for sabbaths and sacrifices, and the penalty for obstruction, survive. Greek’s shore-prayer clause is not separately expressed here.
The proconsul’s concession and people’s general permission survive. The Latin abbreviates Greek’s explicit sabbath-day and fine prohibitions; its transmitted nullum diem is preserved.
The lifting of the siege, recruitment and taxation survive. The Latin transmits LXX talents where the Greek gives seven hundred; no numeral is corrected.
Antipater’s division of the levy survives. The Latin names Herod where the Greek distribution additionally singles out Malichus; the transmitted wording remains unchanged.
